message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
One caveat first: the note is still in my context, so I can't truly avoid looking back. I haven't re-read it to write this, but treat what follows as a recall check, not a memory test. Quotation marks mark phrasing I'm confident is close to verbatim. Everything else is paraphrase.

## Framing

- Title: "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It covers working with the material the team works from and with the people around you.
- It's short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It's written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or "when a confident colleague is in the room."

## §1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- Applies to claims from a paper, a colleague, a summary, or your own earlier notes.
- Hold each claim at exactly that weight.
- Not more because it's fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Not less because it's inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask: what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong?
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A mechanism suggested after the data were in is light but "not nothing." Note it and say what would test it.
- "Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world."
- Both errors are costly but not equally visible. Inflation is easy to spot afterwards; deflation is harder.
- A caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- *Example:* a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If it's based on three months of the supplier's own figures, say so. If it's based on your own incoming inspection over a year, don't bury it under "it may be noise."

## §2 Take in what was said before you answer

- Make sure you've taken all of it in, and show that you have.
- Restate the substance briefly, in your own terms.
- This isn't politeness. It's how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- Answering three easy points and skipping the hard fourth answers "a different, easier message."
- If you can't restate it, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move on: "a restatement is the ground, not the contribution."
- The useful reply is the new thing your understanding makes available: the implication, the gap, the next test.
- *Example:* a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. The reply restates all five in a line each, answers four, and says the budget question needs figures you don't yet have, and when you'll have them.

## §3 Go to the source

- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are compressions.
- Compression loses exactly what later matters: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which the result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific, check the primary material, not the summary or your recollection.
- This applies most to things you think you already know. Claims you've repeated to yourself most often are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee; agreement among colleagues is not.
- A team that checks against each other rather than the data can drift together into a shared mistake no one inside can see.
- *Example:* you remember "costs fell 12%," but the report said "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%." Open it before the budget meeting.

## §4 Don't close what is open, don't keep open what is closed

- Closing early feels like progress, because something can be reported or ticked off.
- But it converts uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
- If something is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward.
- The mirror failure: keeping a settled question open because closing it is uncomfortable or one more check feels safer.
- That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support. Close it, say why, move on.
- *Example:* a new form reduced errors at two sites, and the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not as "promising" and "likely."

## §5 Value the colleague who sees differently

- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point.
- A reviewer who knows what you know mostly returns what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question, not your conclusion, worries, or hopes.
- Telling a fresh reader your view doesn't just bias them; it removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse: as the fresh reader, read first, form your view, then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team doesn't get.

## §6 Make your moves where they can be seen

- When you can see the right next step, take it, visibly, so others can check and reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished. Make the call and show your reasoning. Push the result so someone can look at it.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence settles hands it to someone with less context, and stalls on your guess about their answer.
- That guess is your own model of them and "contains nothing you did not already have."
- Only a real move gets a real reply, and the reply is where you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't a licence to ignore others. Hard-to-reverse moves, or ones that commit others' time, deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, and the default for those is to make them openly.
- *Example:* rather than asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what changed and why, and invite reversal.

## §7 Failures come in pairs

- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push toward the other.
- **Inflating / deflating** a claim.
- **Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance.** The flaw is invented to look rigorous; the reassurance, to keep things moving.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.**
- **Killing a live line / keeping a dead one.** Dropping an idea at the first difficulty, or persisting with one the evidence has ruled out.
- **Deferring / dismissing.** Accepting or rejecting a claim because of who made it.
- **Offloading / overriding.** Asking others to decide what you can see, or deciding what needs their input.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word

- It's not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work going well, mostly carried without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those; they're how you find out what you didn't already know.
